reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of pyrimidine catabolism caused by deficiency of dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase, the first and rate-limiting enzyme degrading uracil and thymine
The most clinically important consequence is severe, sometimes fatal, toxicity from fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy (5-fluorouracil and its prodrug capecitabine)
Because DPD normally clears the great majority of administered fluorouracil, deficient patients accumulate active drug and suffer profound myelosuppression, mucositis, diarrhoea, and neurotoxicity
Constitutional (non-drug) presentations range from asymptomatic carriers to a paediatric encephalopathic phenotype with developmental delay, seizures and hypotonia
The biochemical signature is raised uracil and thymine in urine, plasma and cerebrospinal fluid
Pre-treatment DPYD genotyping and/or measurement of the uracil-to-dihydrouracil ratio identifies at-risk patients before fluoropyrimidine exposure

In deficient patients fluoropyrimidines should be avoided or given at substantially reduced exposure with close monitoring; uridine triacetate is the rescue therapy for established overdose or severe early toxicity
reference.pathophysiology: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase catalyses the rate-limiting first step in the degradation of the pyrimidine bases uracil and thymine. Deficiency causes accumulation of these bases and their precursors in body fluids. Clinically, the disorder has two faces. As an inborn error it can cause a variable neurological phenotype, thought to relate to accumulated metabolites and, in some, associated abnormalities of the neurotransmitter pool. More importantly for adult medicine, fluoropyrimidine drugs are analogues of uracil that are normally inactivated by this enzyme; when it is deficient, the active drug and its cytotoxic metabolites persist, producing severe dose-related toxicity even at standard doses.
additionalDifferentials: Other pyrimidine degradation defects (dihydropyrimidinase and beta-ureidopropionase deficiency)
Chemotherapy toxicity from causes other than DPD deficiency
Other inherited metabolic epileptic encephalopathies in the paediatric phenotype
Drug interactions or overdose accounting for severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity
Sepsis or mucositis of other cause during chemotherapy
Thiamine or other deficiency states causing neurological decline
additionalInvestigations: DPYD genotyping for the common deleterious variants before fluoropyrimidine therapy
Plasma uracil concentration or uracil-to-dihydrouracil ratio as a phenotype test
DPD enzyme activity assay in peripheral blood mononuclear cells where available
Cerebrospinal fluid pyrimidine analysis in the neurological phenotype
Monitoring of full blood count and mucosal/gastrointestinal toxicity during any fluoropyrimidine exposure
redFlags: Rapid, severe myelosuppression, mucositis or diarrhoea early in a fluoropyrimidine course
Neurotoxicity such as encephalopathy or cerebellar signs during chemotherapy
Planned fluoropyrimidine treatment in a patient not yet tested for DPD deficiency
Progressive neurological deterioration in an affected child
reference.prognosis: Constitutional cases range from entirely asymptomatic to significant neurodevelopmental impairment; the critical determinant of outcome is recognition before fluoropyrimidine exposure, since unrecognised deficiency can cause life-threatening or fatal drug toxicity.
pitfalls: Giving standard-dose fluoropyrimidines without checking DPD status
Assuming a normal genotype excludes deficiency, as phenotype testing may add information
Attributing severe early chemotherapy toxicity to chance rather than to enzyme deficiency
Failing to use the specific antidote promptly when severe toxicity occurs
Overlooking that heterozygous partial deficiency can still cause serious toxicity
